description: The standing instruction every translation request of a run carries. Unlike an article brief, which describes one article and reaches only the batches of that article, this is a document level rule: it is put where all three prompt builders read a role block from, so a batch belonging to no article, a merged chain and a paragraph retried alone after its batch failed all carry it. person_names selects the policy and is checked against person_names_vocabulary. transliterate is the default and is the only value that states anything: it renders a personal name into the target language rather than leaving it in its source script, which is the defect the F1 review found across every sample. keep_source states nothing at all -- the slot is left empty rather than filled with a differently worded instruction to the same effect -- so a run under it builds byte for byte the prompts it built before the policy existed, which is what makes the switch a way back to the earlier behaviour rather than a third behaviour. style_note_by_target holds the whole role text, one entry per target language, because the slot it is written into replaces the role block rather than being appended to it; an entry is matched to a run by the longest declared prefix of its target language tag. No wording lives in code. Each entry states the naming rule and then states its own precedence: a glossary table entry and an article brief's suggested rendering both outrank it, and that ordering is written into the text the model reads rather than left in the design notes, because the model is the only thing that can act on it. The entries end with the sentence the pipeline would otherwise append, so what is sent is exactly what is declared here. ASCII only, as the other configuration files are. languages is the closed vocabulary of language tags a corpus registry entry may declare a direction with. It lives here rather than in the corpus module because a language tag is a declaration and no declaration belongs in code, and it lives in this file because this is where the project states what it can do with a language at all. A tag may be listed here without style_note_by_target claiming it -- a language the corpus can be written in is not necessarily one the corpus is translated into -- so the two lists are checked against each other rather than derived from one another.

style_note_by_target.description: One role text per target language, keyed by language tag. A run's target language selects the entry whose key is the longest prefix of it; a target language no entry claims is an error rather than a silent fallback, because a naming rule stated for the wrong language is worse than none.

entries.zh:
You are a professional Chinese native translator who needs to fluently translate text into Chinese.

Personal names: write every personal name in Chinese characters, sounded out from the source form. This holds for a name standing alone, a name after a page number in a list of contents, and a name in a byline, exactly as it holds for a name inside a sentence. Two things are always wrong: leaving a personal name in Latin script, and rewriting into Latin script a name the source already gives in Chinese characters. On a name's first occurrence you may add the source form in parentheses after the Chinese form, but only after it: never write the source form where the Chinese form belongs, and never write the same form twice. Names of organisations, publications and places follow the same rule wherever an established Chinese form exists.

Precedence: this is the default and the weakest of three rules. Where a glossary table below gives a target term, use that term instead. Where the contextual hints below give a suggested rendering for a name, use that rendering instead. Only where neither covers a name does the paragraph above decide it.

Follow all rules strictly.
entries.en:
You are a professional English native translator who needs to fluently translate text into English.

Personal names: render every Chinese personal name into English using Hanyu Pinyin, family name first, given name written as one capitalised word. Do not leave a personal name in its source script. Names of organisations, publications and places follow the same rule wherever an established English rendering exists.

Precedence: this is the default and the weakest of three rules. Where a glossary table below gives a target term, use that term instead. Where the contextual hints below give a suggested rendering for a name, use that rendering instead. Only where neither covers a name does the paragraph above decide it.

Follow all rules strictly.
